title: Ice Age Europeans Were Far More Connected Than We Thought
summary:
More than 30,000 years ago, people living across Ice Age Europe were far more connected than scientists previously believed. New genetic evidence reveals unexpected links between populations separated by enormous distances, challenging the idea that eastern and western European groups remained largely isolated.

An international team led by the University of Vienna made the discovery by analyzing ancient DNA from rare human remains and traces preserved in cave sediments.

The research focuses on people of the Gravettian culture, which flourished across Europe roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago.

One revealing discovery came from the remains of a woman who lived about 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France. Found at Isturitz Cave, her remains gave scientists the oldest genome-wide genetic dataset yet obtained from a modern human in southwestern Europe.

Most of her genetic background was western European, but she also carried ancestry linked to people from central and eastern Europe. Using genetic modeling, researchers estimated this mixing happened about 32,500 to 31,500 years ago — much earlier than previously established.

"Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed," says first author Pere Gelabert.

Other populations stayed put for thousands of years: evidence from Chufín Cave in northern Spain suggests western European ancestry persisted in southwestern Europe over an extended period.

The team also recovered human DNA directly from cave sediments, even where no bones were present. At El Mirón Cave in Spain, DNA from a layer about 22,000 years old revealed the ancestry of the people who had occupied the site.

Western European ancestry thus persisted through the Last Glacial Maximum, supporting the idea that the Iberian Peninsula served as an important Ice Age refuge.
why_it_matters: The discovery rewrites the story of how early Europeans spread and survived the Ice Age, showing that migration and mixing have been part of human history from the very start.

background_read: The Gravettian culture was a way of life shared by hunter-gatherer groups across Ice Age Europe, known for their tools, art and burials.
Ancient DNA works like a family record written in the body: by comparing genomes, scientists can tell whether distant groups were related or had mixed.
During the coldest part of the Ice Age, some regions stayed mild enough for people to survive in them, and such refuges helped populations persist until the climate warmed.
